I recommended a right index trigger finger cortisone injection today, and the patient elected to proceed. Urinary incontinence.
Adult hydrocephalus.

Cognitive impairment.

• Constitutional Symptoms: Significant for impaired ability to carry out daily functions. Negative for fever or unintentional weight loss.

Constitutional

• Adult hydrocephalus.
• Gait impairment.
• Urinary incontinence and urgency.
• Cognitive impairment.

I had a long discussion with the patient and his daughter. Final pathology report of the biopsy is pending, however preliminary report is suggestive of malignancy, most likely lymphoma. Surgery was consulted and discussed with the patient the possiblity of going to surgery for resection of the area. Currently, the patient is not interested in going to surgery. The fact that this surgery would be palliative was explained to the patiend and his wife. However, they wish to defer surgery at this time. They have been told that the patient is at risk of further bleeding and/or obstruction without this surgery and that surgery would, in many ways, be palliative. PRE-SYNCOPE: Her history was most consistent with medication induced pre-syncope. She is on several medications that can cause somnolence or orthostasis including fentnyl, ativan, percocet, prazosin, and oxybutynin. A sub-dural hematoma was a consideration given her recent head trauma as well as metastases from her potential lung cancer, but a CT head without contrast was negative for any acute abnormality. Cardiac syncope was less likely from her history, but she was still ruled out with no abnormality seen on telemetry. There was no evidence of infection or electrolyte abnormality and a urine culture was negative. She did not have any further episodes after discontinuoing her lorazepam and prazosin. If she were to have future episodes, one could consider performing an EEG or an MRI of her head to rule out micro-metastases from her probable lung cancer. . #. HYPERTENSION: She was on an unusual home regimen, including metoprolol 50mg qAM, 25mg qPM, and prazosin. When asked if she had been on any other blood pressure medications in the past, she mentioned she had been on methyldopa but nothing else. Her prazosin was discontinued and she was started on HCTZ 12.5mg daily which will likely need to be uptitrated as an outpatient. . #. human_summary: Mr. ___ was admitted to the Urology Service after undergoing robotic assisted laparoscopic simple prostatectomy. No concerning intra-operative events occurred; please see dictated operative note for full details. The patient received ___ antibiotic prophylaxis. At the end of the procedure the patient was extubated and transported to the PACU for further recovery before being transferred to the floor. He was transferred from the PACU in stable condition. On POD0, pain was well controlled on PCA, hydrated with intravenous fluids for urine output >30cc/hour, provided with pneumoboots and incentive spirometry for prophylaxis, and he ambulated once. On POD1, the patient was restarted on home medications, basic metabolic panel and complete blood count were checked, pain control was transitioned from PCA to oral analgesics, diet was advanced to a clears/toast and crackers diet for breakfast and lunch. Diet was advanced to regular after lunch and with further ambulation, the JP drain was removed. Patient was concerned about ability to move around at home and was bothered by bladder spasms during his hospital course. His catheter drained clear punch colored urine without clots and was irrigated on several occasions with no signs of obstruction. He continued to have intermittent bladder spasms despite oxybutynin, pyridium and PO valium and these continued to improve over the course of his hospital stay. Of note his blood pressure post-operatively was elevated into 180s. He was resumed on his home medications and had additional PO hydralazine administered x1. Hypertension was discussed with medicine team who agreed that additional time with home medications would be effective and ultimately his BP did come down to the 130s by day of discharge. He continued to feel well from a cardiac standpoint with no symptoms. Foley catheter care and leg bag teaching was provided by nursing. The remainder of the hospital course was unremarkable. The patient was discharged in stable condition, eating well, ambulating independently, and with pain control on oral analgesics. On exam, incision was clean, dry, and intact, with no evidence of hematoma collection or infection. The patient was given explicit instructions to follow-up in one week for post-operative evaluation and trial of voiding.

Her GIB was thought to be secondary to diverticulosis, and a tagged RBC was performed and confirmed bleeding from the sigmoid colon. An angiography was subsequently performed to embolize the bleeding vessels but the patient was no longer actively bleeding at the time of this study, and no embolization was done. She received six units of PRBC in the MICU and her Hct improved to 36. It remained stable for the five days she remained in the hospital after her last transfusion. She continued to have scant bleeding per rectum, however. This was discussed with the GI consult service, and they recommended a colonoscopy on an inpatient or outpatient basis, but were not concerned about acute bleeding because of her stable hematocrit. She will follow-up with GI after discharge (an appointment has been made). Her aspirin was also discontinued but the patient and her niece were instructed that the re-initiation of aspirin could be discussed in the future with the patient's primary care doctor. If the patient has any further episodes of GIB at rehab, please check her hematocrit and call her PCP, ___, ___, to share the results. # UTI - The patient had a foley catheter inserted in her bladder when she arrived in the MICU. and her urine was noted to be immediately opaque. A urinalysis showed many bacteria and she was started on ceftriaxone for a presumed UTI. Her urine eventually grew E. coli that was sensitive to ceftriaxone and cipro. She received a total of three days of antibiotics for an uncomplicated UTI, as her infection was already active before the insertion of the foley. # Right basillic vein thrombus: The patient developed a thrombus of the right basillic vein as a result of peripheral IV access. MEDICATIONS: Unless told otherwise you should resume taking all of the medications you were taking before surgery. You will be given a new prescription for pain medication, which can be taken every three (3) to four (4) hours only if necessary. Eat small balanced meals throughout the day. CAUTIONS: NO SMOKING! We know you've heard this before, but it really is an important step to your recovery. Smoking causes narrowing of your blood vessels which in turn decreases circulation. If you smoke you will need to stop as soon as possible. Ask your nurse or doctor for information on smoking cessation. Avoid pressure to your amputation site. No strenuous activity for 6 weeks after surgery. For people with vascular problems we would recommend a cholesterol lowering diet: Follow a diet low in total fat and low in saturated fat and in cholesterol to improve lipid profile in your blood. Additionally, some people see a reduction in serum cholesterol by reducing dietary cholesterol. Since a reduction in dietary cholesterol is not harmful, we suggest that most people reduce dietary fat, saturated fat and cholesterol to decrease total cholesterol and LDL (Low Density Lipoprotein-the bad cholesterol). Exercise will increase your HDL (High Density Lipoprotein-the good cholesterol) and with your doctor's permission, is typically recommended. You may be self-referred or get a referral from your doctor. If you are overweight, you need to think about starting a weight management program. Your health and its improvement depend on it. PAIN MANAGEMENT:
It is normal to feel some discomfort/pain following abdominal 
surgery. This pain is often described as "soreness". 
Your pain should get better day by day. If you find the pain is 
getting worse instead of better, please contact your surgeon.
You will receive a prescription from your surgeon for pain 
medicine to take by mouth. It is important to take this medicine 
as directied. Do not take it more frequently than prescribed. Do 
not take more medicine at one time than prescribed.
Your pain medicine will work better if you take it before your 
pain gets too severe.
Talk with your surgeon about how long you will need to take 
prescription pain medicine. Please don't take any other pain 
medicine, including non-prescription pain medicine, unless your 
surgeon has said its okay.
If you are experiencing no pain, it is okay to skip a dose of 
pain medicine.
Remember to use your "cough pillow" for splinting when you cough 
or when you are doing your deep breathing exercises.
If you experience any of the folloiwng, please contact your 
surgeon:
- sharp pain or any severe pain that lasts several hours
- pain that is getting worse over time
- pain accompanied by fever of more than 101
- a drastic change in nature or quality of your pain
 
MEDICATIONS:
Take all the medicines you were on before the operation just as 
you did before, unless you have been told differently.
If you have any questions about what medicine to take or not to 
take, please call your surgeon.
 
DANGER SIGNS:
Please call your surgeon if you develop:
- worsening abdominal pain
- sharp or severe pain that lasts several hours
- temperature of 101 degrees or higher
- severe diarrhea
- vomiting
- redness around the incision that is spreading
- increased swelling around the incision
- excessive bruising around the incision
- cloudy fluid coming from the wound
- bright red blood or foul smelling discharge coming from the 
wound
- an increase in drainage from the wound

It is normal to feel some discomfort/pain following abdominal 
surgery. This pain is often described as "soreness". 
Your pain should get better day by day. If you find the pain is

medicine to take by mouth. It is important to take this medicine 
as directied. Do not take it more frequently than prescribed. Do 
not take more medicine at one time than prescribed.
Your pain medicine will work better if you take it before your 
pain gets too severe.
Talk with your surgeon about how long you will need to take 
prescription pain medicine. Please don't take any other pain 
medicine, including non-prescription pain medicine, unless your 
surgeon has said its okay.
IF you are experiencing no pain, it is okay to skip a dose of 
pain medicine.
Remember to use your "cough pillow" for splinting when you cough 
or when you are doing your deep breathing exercises.
